title: Could an Artificial-Intelligence agent pass an introductory physics course?
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT, a large language model, could successfully complete the kinds of assessments used in a standard introductory calculus-based undergraduate physics course. The core question is not only whether the AI can obtain passing scores, but also whether its errors resemble those of beginning physics students. The author frames the study in the context of growing concern about AI in education, especially around cheating, misinformation, and the implications for physics instruction.

To investigate this, the author entered representative course assessment materials into ChatGPT and evaluated its performance as if it were a student in the course. The materials came from first-year calculus-based physics courses previously taught by the author at Michigan State University and included a Force Concept Inventory, online homework, clicker questions, programming exercises, and a final exam. ChatGPT’s January 9, 2023 version was used. The AI was allowed different levels of interaction depending on the task: multiple attempts and dialogue for homework and programming, replayed peer-instruction discussion for clicker questions, and only a first response for exams. Figures and graphs had to be transcribed into text because the system was text-based.

The context is undergraduate physics education at a single university course sequence. The paper does not study human learners as the main analytic unit; rather, it benchmarks ChatGPT against the structure, standards, and grading practices of the course, while drawing comparisons to common novice student misconceptions. The instructor-author serves as evaluator, grader, and prompt provider throughout the study.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT would narrowly pass the course overall, earning an estimated course grade of 1.5 out of 4.0 under a typical weighting scheme. It performed relatively well on concept inventory and clicker questions, extremely well on programming tasks, and poorly on exams and many numerical calculations. The author argues that ChatGPT often displays the same conceptual errors and unproductive guessing patterns seen in beginning learners, but lacks metacognition and presents incorrect reasoning with confidence. The paper concludes that the key educational issue is less AI-enabled cheating and more how physics education should adapt to a future in which students and professionals work alongside AI systems.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's large language model chatbot that generates human-like text responses and explanations across domains, including physics problem solving and code generation.
identified_tools.use_case: ChatGPT was tested on representative assessments from an introductory calculus-based physics course, including the Force Concept Inventory, homework, clicker questions, a programming exercise, and a final exam, with responses graded as student work would be graded.

findings.finding_summary: On the Force Concept Inventory, ChatGPT scored 18/30 (60%), which the author interprets as corresponding to the suggested entry threshold for Newtonian physics. The paper reports that ChatGPT showed common novice-like physics misconceptions, including impetus reasoning and confusion between individual and net forces.

Across 76 homework problems, ChatGPT solved 55% correctly using an average of 1.88 attempts. Performance varied by topic: 48% on trajectory motion and friction, 68% on thermodynamics, 62% on capacitance, and 36% on special relativity; the author attributes much of the difficulty to numerical and algebraic manipulation errors, especially with square roots.

On clicker questions from a momentum lecture, ChatGPT correctly solved 10 of 12 questions. Under the course's participation-based clicker grading policy, this would yield a 93% clicker score, reportedly better than most students in the actual course, though the paper notes students were learning new concepts while ChatGPT was already pretrained.

In a VPython programming exercise, ChatGPT initially produced code with errors, but after one corrective prompt it generated a working program, and after a third prompt it added the bonus graphing feature. The author reports that this would earn full credit plus bonus (120%) and that ChatGPT performed better than any students in the course on this component.

On the mechanics final exam, ChatGPT scored 14/30 (47%) by answer correctness. The author estimates that with hand grading and partial credit, the score would have been between 46% and 50%, because some wrong answers came from numerical errors while some correct answers reflected flawed reasoning.

Using a typical course weighting of 20% homework, 5% clicker, 5% programming, and 70% exams, ChatGPT's overall course score would be 54.55%, corresponding to a grade of 1.5. The paper concludes this would be enough for course credit but below the 2.0 grade-point average needed for graduation, and suggests improved numerical functionality could raise performance to a 2.0-grade level.

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical single-paper evaluation of one tool on authentic course assessments, but it is essentially a case study with anecdotal elements, no comparison group, and no student sample or causal design. The author explicitly describes the methodology as strictly empirical and arguably anecdotal.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows mixed performance: ChatGPT narrowly passes the course simulation overall, performs strongly on clicker questions and programming, but only moderately on homework and poorly on the exam. Because no standardized causal effect size on learners is reported and impacts are uneven across measures, impact is best classified as unclear/mixed.
